_README: Round 2 of the source-citation removal: 19 columns whose attribution survived round 1 because that pass’s pattern ended in \b, so “Beckey’s guidebook” could not match.

set.overview: Anderson's Thumb is a sharp rock spire on the Mount Anderson massif in the central Olympics, near Echo Rock and Flypaper Pass. Reaching it requires a long approach and glacier travel on the Eel Glacier - the Anderson Glacier on the south side of the massif disappeared by roughly 2011 and is now bare rock/moraine rather than crevassed ice. The spire itself is exposed Class 4 to low-5th-class climbing on good Olympic sandstone - a small but committing technical summit.

set.approach: From the Entiat River Trailhead (3,150 ft, end of Entiat River Road), follow the Entiat River Trail #1400, a well-graded but increasingly rough valley trail that parallels the Entiat River the entire way. At 2.2 miles (3,480 ft) the Anthem Creek Trail #1435 splits off; the crossing at 2.5 miles is on a solid wooden bridge. At 3.6 miles (3,745 ft) pass the Cow Creek Meadows/Myrtle Lake Trail #1404 junction, then the Larch Lakes Trail #1430 at 4.7 miles (3,780 ft), Snowy Creek Meadows around 6.1 miles, and the Emerald Park Trail #1230 junction at 6.2 miles (4,000 ft). Miles 6-12 cross repeated burn zones from the Tinpan (2006), Wolverine (2015) and Duncan Ridge (2014) fires — expect an exposed, dry, dusty tread with little shade. At 8.2 miles (4,330 ft) pass the Ice Creek Trail #1405 junction, and reach Entiat Meadows proper around 11 miles (4,600 ft), a good camp with reliable water. Continue past the Cool Creek Trail #1431 junction at 13.3 miles (5,060 ft) into upper Entiat Meadows; the trail grows faint and brush/deadfall-choked above about 14 miles as it nears timberline (roughly 14.5-14.8 miles, ~5,100 ft), the usual base camp for the peak. From camp, leave the trail and climb the open, south-facing slope/rib system directly below Buckskin's summit — this is a broad old avalanche path; the rib closest to camp carries the least brush and gives the most direct line, while an old, badly overgrown boot path toward the east ridge is generally not worth chasing due to extensive deadfall. Ascend scree and heather (loose, will be slick when wet) roughly 2,000-2,800 ft to gain the east ridge around 7,200-7,900 ft, then follow the ridge crest — narrow and blocky in spots with minor gendarmes — the final few hundred feet to the 8,127 ft summit. Water is reliable along the entire valley trail (Entiat River, Anthem Creek at 2.2 mi, Snowybrushy Creek around 5.2 mi, plus seasonal side streams) but there is no dependable water above the meadows once you leave the trail, aside from early-season snowmelt. Main approach-specific hazards: heat/sun exposure through the burn sections, navigation through deadfall on the upper trail and on any attempt at the old east-ridge boot path, and loose, ball-bearing scree and wet heather on the open slope below the ridge.

set.descent_text: Reverse the climbing route from the summit rather than continuing over the north ridge. Down-climb the loose, exposed class 4-5 summit ridge and ledges just south of the true summit using running belays and gear placements — this terrain is horribly loose, so treat every hold as suspect and keep the rope short between placements. At the top of the crux headwall, make one single-strand rappel down the ~10-ft near-vertical crack (roughly 5.8+ or 5.2/A1); a single 30-40m rope reaches the ledge below. Continue down and along the loose class 4-5 ledges around the north ridge's pinnacles to a rock horn draped with old rappel slings (do not trust weathered fixed tat — back it up with your own cord); from this horn, make two rappels on doubled ropes (a party in 2020 used a 40m and 30m 6.9mm alpine rope joined together) to reach an exit ledge above the couloir — a single 60m rope doubled, or two 30m ropes, works as a substitute. From the exit ledge, down-climb the 40-45° northwest snow couloir, placing snow pickets or flukes as protection if conditions are firm or icy, back to the saddle just north of the peak and down to camp on the Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine. From camp, reverse the full glaciated approach (Challenger Glacier, West Challenger Notch, Perfect Pass, Whatcom Glacier traverse, Whatcom Pass, Brush Creek Trail, Chilliwack River Trail and cable car, Hannegan Pass) back to the Hannegan Trailhead. All anchors encountered are natural/fixed-sling (horn or gear) — there is no bolted rappel line on this route. Total rappel count: 3 (one at the headwall crack, two from the north-ridge horn).

From the top, one option is to traverse a short catwalk and build rappel anchors roughly 100 feet west of the true summit; another option is to rappel north until you can cross the gully separating Minuteman from Liberty Bell, then downclimb to a bush anchor for a final rappel. Either way, about three rappels on a single 60m rope typically regain the approach talus. Existing fixed slings around horns/blocks should be inspected (and backed up if in doubt) before weighting, since they're exposed to UV and rockfall.

set.approach: Four Brothers sits on Chikamin Ridge in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness, and the standard approach starts at the Mineral Creek Trailhead (Trail #1331, ~2,375 ft), reached via SR 903 north from Cle Elum ~17 mi, then Cooper Lake Rd/FR-46 roughly 9-10 mi to the signed trailhead. From the trailhead the trail drops briefly to a crossing of the Kachess River, then climbs to a junction with the Little Kachess Trail (#1312) at about 0.25 mi. Around 1.3 mi it passes an old mine site and shortly after crosses Mineral Creek itself, entering the Alpine Lakes Wilderness boundary. The next stretch runs high above the creek through old-growth forest and several brushy former avalanche paths - expect deadfall and slow going here, especially early season. Near the 4-mile mark the trail crosses a side creek (the last dependable water before the basin) and then climbs steeply, gaining roughly 1,500 ft in the final mile-plus to Upper Park Lake (~4,900 ft, about 5.4 mi from the trailhead). From the Park Lakes basin, leave the trail and go cross-country up mixed heather benches and slabby rock toward the saddle on Chikamin Ridge, staying to the north side of the Four Brothers - the four cliffy summit points are unmistakable and form steep, technical terrain that should be flanked rather than climbed directly from below. Once on the ridge crest, traverse back to the base of the southwest-facing gully/slope system that gives this route its name, roughly 6.5-7 mi and about 4,000 ft of gain from the car. Expect lingering snow in the gully well into July, loose stacked talus higher up, and real routefinding complexity picking a line through the pinnacle/cliff-band maze - this is the part of the outing that most often proves the crux, more so than any single move.

Two approaches are used, both longer and more involved than the standard Sitkum route. (1) Via White Chuck River Trailhead (2,300 ft): follow the White Chuck River Trail (FST 643) about 6 miles to the Kennedy Ridge Trail (FST 639) junction, then Kennedy Ridge Trail 1.7 miles up to the PCT. Head north on the PCT about 3 miles (roughly 0.7 miles past the Kennedy Creek crossing, a water source) to an unmarked climbers' path leaving the PCT, which climbs snow and pumice to the standard high camp near 7,200 ft on the Kennedy Ridge shoulder. (2) Via North Fork Sauk Trailhead: North Fork Sauk Trail to White Pass (~9 miles, ~5,900 ft), then a long traverse north on/near the PCT to the same Kennedy Ridge camp area — a 20-mile-plus approach day used by some parties. From high camp, the route proper begins by traversing the upper southwest slopes of the Ptarmigan Glacier just below the ridgeline to about 8,000 ft, rounding Kennedy Peak to an 8,000 ft saddle between the Vista and Kennedy Glaciers. Ascend the Kennedy Glacier — a 'crumbling mess' of loose moraine and boulders low down — to an 8,800 ft saddle where Frostbite Ridge proper begins. The ridge itself mixes loose pumice/dust scrambling on narrow, exposed steps with sections of steep snow (45–50°) protected with pickets or ice screws, passing directly beneath/through the Rabbit Ears — twin eroded lava pinnacles — where loose rock is a real hazard, especially in warm, dry conditions (cold, snowy conditions lock the rock in place and make the scramble more manageable). Above the Rabbit Ears the route steepens further into a section of alpine ice, anywhere from a single ~40-foot ice step to roughly 200 feet of AI2, typically simul-climbed with ice screw protection, before crossing the crater rim and descending briefly into the crater to reach the 10,550 ft summit.

set.beta: A moderate, multi-pitch line following the arête on the mountain's northeast side. The rock looks classic but climbs 'shaky,' with numerous fragile flakes of dubious stability and protection that is sometimes insecure.

A climber reached roughly 60% of the route on a third try before retreating, free-climbing a crux pitch that earlier parties had aided. The second ascent, in 1998, involved a summit-day round trip of about 12 hours from bivouac back to the car. Treat all of this as thin, second-hand history rather than current beta.

set.overview: A Grade IV, 5.9 technical rock route on the North Peak's west face, very difficult to protect and among the hardest routes on the mountain.

set.descent_text: There is no walk-off from the top of the north ridge/north face — it's a rappelling descent back down steep, often loose terrain. Because the north face has no established independent descent line, parties either reverse the ridge/face itself or (more commonly, per the pattern typical of routes like this) traverse over on the upper mountain to descend the easier, well-traveled southwest gully (the 'X Couloir' used as the standard route's descent) rather than rappel the full north face a second time. Reversing the route means building rappel anchors off slung rock horns and blocks through the steepest ice and mixed sections — the rock here is loose, so test anchors and blocks carefully and avoid pulling ropes across bare rock edges. Given the face is roughly 1,000 ft (~300m) of sustained steep ground, and using a single rope doubled (~30m per rappel) is the standard setup for anchors of this type, expect on the order of 4-6 rappels through the steepest ice/mixed sections with some downclimbing or simul-climbing on the more moderate snow between them if descending the face directly; if instead you traverse to the standard SW gully, expect a rappel sequence similar to that route's (commonly up to 10 double-rope rappels off a mix of pickets and existing horn slings, conditions-dependent). Either way, re-rope once back on the Coleman Glacier for the crevassed descent back to the Hogsback moraine and the Heliotrope Ridge Trail.

set.overview: Monte Cristo Peak (7,136 ft) is the technical centerpiece of the Monte Cristo Group, a tight cluster of peaks (Kyes, Cadet, Columbia, Del Campo) ringing the ghost town of Monte Cristo in the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness. Unlike its neighbors, Monte Cristo has no scramble-only line to the true summit: the standard and most-climbed route, the North Col Route, requires roped 5.6 rock climbing through a short chimney above the col, so it's properly a Basic Alpine Climb rather than a Class 3 scramble. The peak was first climbed in 1923 by James M. Keyes and W. Zerum, and in 1918 was called 'a huge pile of red rock.'

set.descent_text: Standard descent is the North Ridge (also called the North Cleaver) or the adjacent snowfield beside it, dropping back toward High Camp — this is a walk-off/downclimb, not a rappel route. It is the least pleasant part of the trip: long stretches of loose, rotten volcanic scree and boulders, occasional narrow/exposed sections, and a real chance of rockfall onto parties below, so groups should spread out and move quickly through the worst of it. No fixed anchors or rappels are used on the standard line; a short rope-assisted downclimb over an isolated rock band is occasionally used by parties uncomfortable with exposure, but this is improvised, not a bolted or standard rappel. Once back at High Camp, retrace the High Camp Trail and Killen Creek Trail to the trailhead. Some parties instead descend the South Climb route to the Cold Springs trailhead, which requires a car shuttle or a long road walk back to Killen Creek since it's a different trailhead entirely.

set.overview: Mount Degenhardt (8,107 ft) is a remote Southern Pickets summit at the north end of The Barrier, between Mount Terror and Inspiration Peak, with the Terror Glacier on its southeast flank. Named for William Degenhardt, an early Cascades pioneer who made the first ascent in 1931 with Herbert Strandberg. It's widely regarded as the chossiest peak in the Southern Pickets — loose, fractured gneiss throughout — but rewards the effort with a striking, rarely-visited summit and views across Crescent Creek and Terror Basin.

set.approach: There is no dedicated trailhead, road, or maintained path to Mount Ferry — reaching it means committing to 2-3 days of the Bailey Range Traverse, Olympic National Park's classic off-trail high route that links the Sol Duc River trailhead (via Sol Duc Falls Trail #630) in the north with the Elwha River/Whiskey Bend trailhead in the south, or with the North Fork Quinault trailhead via Dodwell-Rixon Pass on the longer loop variant. The most common approach starts at the Sol Duc Trailhead: maintained trail runs about 1 mile to Sol Duc Falls, then climbs steadily past Deer Lake and up the High Divide Trail toward Bogachiel Peak/Heart Lake — roughly 9-11 miles and ~3,300 ft of gain from the car, and the last reliable on-trail water and camp before travel goes off-trail. From High Divide near Cat Basin, the route leaves the maintained trail and follows the Bailey Range crest east: over Cat Peak's exposed 'Catwalk' (an airy class 3 knife-edge ridge, the first of two such sections on the traverse) and Stephen Peak, where steep heather benches with class 3-4 moves lead into a second, brushier catwalk with awkward gully crossings serious enough to warrant a blunt 'DON'T. FALL.' warning before dropping into Ferry Basin (~5,700 ft), the standard camp beneath Mount Ferry and roughly 2 days / 15-20 miles of travel in. Ferry Basin has dependable water — a small waterfall about 60 ft from the usual camp spot, plus a nearby tarn — and is often considered one of the nicer camps on the traverse. From camp, Ferry's summit is reached via a broad bench and scree/talus slope east of the true summit, loose 'dagger scree' (sharp, shifting shale-like rock) that demands careful footing but involves no technical climbing, just sustained off-trail scrambling. A less-common southern approach comes in via Dodwell-Rixon Pass and Queets Basin, up Ball Bearing Gully to the Scott-Ludden saddle, then along the Ferry-Ludden ridge to that same broad bench east of the summit. Either way, expect no signage, no bridges, unmarked creek fords, lingering snow/ice in gullies and on north-facing slopes even in August (ice axe and often crampons are standard kit), slide alder brush lower on the flanks, and serious route-finding responsibility — this is remote, high alpine terrain well beyond the maintained trail network.

set.descent_text: Reverse the ascent line rather than continuing the Iron-Worthington ridge traverse. From the summit plateau, downclimb the short technical step below the true summit -- a class 3-4 face with good holds, done as an 'up-and-down climb' on the same line used to ascend (an alternate, slightly easier low-exposure line exists around the NE corner of the summit block for parties that want to avoid re-downclimbing the ascent face). There are no fixed rappel anchors, bolts, or established rappel stations on this route -- this is a walk-off/downclimb peak, not a rappel route. From the base of the summit block, descend southwest back to the Iron-Worthington col, then drop into the wide scree/talus gully on the west side of the col -- this is the standout feature of the descent, offering a fast, low-angle boot-ski through loose scree and talus back down to treeline and the avalanche-debris bench above Buckhorn Lake. Below treeline, re-cross the inlet stream, pick up the boot path back to the Buckhorn Lake spur, and rejoin the maintained Tubal Cain Trail #840 for the ~5.5-6 mile, ~2,800 ft-loss walk out to the trailhead. Because the summit block is a short, low-exposure downclimb rather than a rappel, and no rope is needed for the descent (a rope is optional/prudent for less confident scramblers on the way up, not for a rappel), rappels = 0.

Reverse the ascent line. Most parties downclimb the same loose south-side gully back to the Dome–Sinister col — it is one of the loosest, most unpleasant sections on the mountain, so expect care-intensive downclimbing with real rockfall risk to anyone below. A commonly preferred alternative, used by several recent parties instead of re-descending the gully, is to descend via the lower west ridge: a newer, more direct line involving sustained Class 3–4 scrambling on semi-solid rock with considerable exposure. One crux move on this ridge variant has a fixed sling left in place for protection/handline use, but this is not a rappel station — parties downclimb through it. Either way, the descent rejoins the gentle snow slopes leading back to the 7,640' Dome–Sinister col. At the col, the bergschrund that guards access to the Chikamin Glacier can be broken/unbridged in mid-to-late season; when it is, parties have used a single rappel (one 60m rope) off natural anchors (rock horn/sling or v-thread in snow, depending on conditions) to get down onto the glacier safely rather than risk a fall into the schrund — in good snow conditions or earlier in the season this same spot is often just a step-across or short downclimb with no rope work needed. From the glacier, re-ascend roughly 1,000' back to the Dome–Chikamin col, then descend to high camp on Itswoot Ridge/Cub Lake and reverse the long Bachelor Creek/Downey Creek trail back to the trailhead. Watch for loose rock in the gully, exposure on the west-ridge variant, and crevasse hazard on the Chikamin/Dome glacier crossings in both directions.

set.approach: The approach is essentially the same as the standard South Face route: from the Snoqualmie Pass PCT-North trailhead (I-90 Exit 52, ~3,000 ft), follow the PCT north about 2.5 miles to the Commonwealth Creek Trail (#1033) junction and follow it into Commonwealth Basin. Shortly after crossing Commonwealth Creek (the last water on the approach), this line stays briefly on the climbers' path along the base of Red Mountain's flank before cutting left (northwest) off-trail into upper Commonwealth Basin to reach the base of Lundin's south face. The variation starts near the center and lowest point of the face, at an obvious layback, hand-sized crack - distinctly different from where the original South Face line starts, so look for the crack itself rather than following old route photos literally. Expect the same cross-country talus/boulder travel and lingering early-season snow in the basin as the standard South Face route.

set.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line rather than any independent walk-off. From the true summit, most parties make three single-rope (30 m) rappels down the tower to a small, exposed high notch, then one longer double-rope (60 m) rappel from that notch down into the gully/glacier below — roughly four rappels in typical late-summer, snow-free conditions. Anchors along this line are almost entirely improvised rather than bolted: slung boulders, horns and pedestals wrapped with tat/cord, and the occasional jammed knot in a crack; a couple of the stations have accumulated enough old cord to look semi-permanent, but none should be trusted blindly and back-up/extend as needed. Bring a single 60 m rope (or two ropes if you want to do the notch-to-glacier drop as one clean pull rather than downclimbing part of it). In seasons or conditions where a snow finger lingers in the descent gully, parties have needed far more — up to 9-10 shorter single-rope rappels interspersed with downclimbing to get through the same 400-ft gully system, because a lingering snow patch prevents a clean full-length pull; budget extra time and a plan B if you find snow still choking the gully. Known hazards on this descent: persistently loose, choss-prone rock (the Southeast Spire's rock quality is poor, and at least one incident involved a slab breaking loose during rope retrieval at the notch and striking a climber), ropes getting stuck when pulled through the loose gully, high exposure along the east ledges near the Ridge of Gendarmes, and fatigue/darkness on the lower-angle terrain given how long this climb runs. After reaching the glacier below the Col of the Wild, reverse the approach traverse back to your high camp (Redoubt Col/Ouzel Lake), then descend the Depot Creek climbers path past the falls — using the fixed handline again on the steep slab section — back to the trailhead.

set.beta: The east face starts around 7,600 ft and climbs a right-trending ramp of class 2-3 slabby scrambling, a short class 4 chimney, and blocky, zigzagging ledges (slow, time-consuming route-finding) to a crux of 1-2 poorly-protected 5.4 moves on a thin flake/crack (the overall route is sometimes graded 5.6), then sustained class 4 terrain for the final ~150 ft summit pitch, easing back to class 3-4 at the top.
